pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Alternaria brassicae and A. brassicicola can infect leaves, petioles, stems, flower parts, and seed pods of a wide range of Brassicaceae crops and weeds.

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the fungal pathogen Alternaria brassicicola

affected_parts.quote: Alternaria brassicae and A. brassicicola can infect leaves, petioles, stems, flower parts, and seed pods of a wide range of Brassicaceae crops and weeds.

summary.value: Small dark or yellow leaf spots first develop, enlarging to circular areas that are brown to gray in color with or without concentric rings (target/bull's-eye lesions), possibly with black or purple borders and/or surrounded by yellow halos. Spots range from pinpoint dots to several millimeters. Yellowing of surrounding tissue and leaf drop may occur. Seed pods show characteristic tiger-striping.
summary.quote: Small, dark or yellow leaf spots first develop, enlarging to circular areas that are brown to gray in color with or without concentric rings and possibly with black or purple borders and/or surrounded by yellow halos... Cabbage seed pods atop leaf show 'tiger-striping' that is characteristic of infections on seed pods.

diagnostic_features.value: Target spots or bull's-eye lesions with concentric rings, yellow halos, and necrotic centers visible from both sides of the leaf. Lesion centers coated with sooty black spore masses that can crack or drop out producing shot holes. Spots may be angular when limited by leaf veins. Seed pods show tiger-striping. Lesions generally do not penetrate deeply into the cauliflower head.
diagnostic_features.quote: Alternaria leaf spot symptoms can include target spots with concentric rings, a yellow halo, and a necrotic center. The lesions are visible from both sides of the leaf and the necrotic lesions can easily tear. Black sooty spores are produced on the surface during extended periods of high humidity.

conflicts.note: Cornell source cites only A. brassicicola; PNW Handbooks and Ohio State cite both A. brassicae and A. brassicicola as causal agents. Canonical value reflects the broader consensus from two sources.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Erwinia carotovora subsp. carotovora (syn. = Pectobacterium carotovorum subsp. carotovorum)

type_of_disease.quote: The soft-rot bacterium, Erwinia carotovora subsp. carotovora

affected_parts.quote: Bacterial soft rots damage succulent plant parts such as fruits, tubers, stems and bulbs

summary.value: Small water-soaked areas appear and rapidly enlarge on plant tissue. Tissue becomes soft and mushy, and within a few days the affected plant part may collapse. Interior tissues become mushy and discolored ranging from cream to black. Seepage from affected areas is common and a strong, disagreeable odor usually is present.
summary.quote: Initially, bacterial soft rots cause water-soaked spots. These spots enlarge over time and become sunken and soft. Interior tissues beneath the spots become mushy and discolored, with the discoloration ranging anywhere from cream to black. Seepage from affected areas is common. Soft rots are known for a strong, disagreeable odor that accompanies the breakdown of plant tissue.

diagnostic_features.value: Water-soaked spots that enlarge and become progressively sunken and soft with mushy discolored interior tissue (cream to black), seepage, and strong disagreeable odor. On cauliflower heads, light brown slimy spots coalesce into larger zones and penetrate deeply into the head. Woody tissues are not susceptible.
diagnostic_features.quote: Initially, bacterial soft rots cause water-soaked spots. These spots enlarge over time and become sunken and soft. Interior tissues beneath the spots become mushy and discolored, with the discoloration ranging anywhere from cream to black. Seepage from affected areas is common. Soft rots are known for a strong, disagreeable odor. Woody tissues are not susceptible.

conflicts.note: Wisconsin Horticulture notes soft rot is caused by multiple bacteria including Pectobacterium carotovorum and Dickeya dadantii; the PNW Handbook and Ohio State source focus on Pectobacterium carotovorum subsp. carotovorum (syn. Erwinia carotovora subsp. carotovora) as primary pathogen on Brassica.

PNW Handbooks uses Erwinia carotovora subsp. carotovora as the primary name with Pectobacterium carotovorum subsp. carotovorum noted as a synonym; current accepted name is Pectobacterium carotovorum subsp. carotovorum.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The disease is caused by the seed-borne bacterium Xanthomonas campestris pv. campetris

type_of_disease.quote: The disease is caused by the seed-borne bacterium

affected_parts.quote: The most common symptom of black rot are yellow, v-shaped lesions that extend toward the base of the leaf that eventually lead to wilt and necrosis... Root crops may not have visible symptoms on above ground tissues, but blackened veins will develop on the roots. As the disease progresses and spreads to the stem, the inner tissue becomes black and the flow of water and nutrients is inhibited leading to plant death.

summary.value: Tissues at leaf margins become yellow with chlorosis progressing toward the leaf center in a V-shaped pattern with the base at the leaf midrib; veins in these areas become dark brown or black and show as a black net when held to light; vascular tissue of the main stem becomes blackened, impairing water and nutrient flow.
summary.quote: Tissues at leaf margins become yellow; chlorosis progresses toward the leaf center, creating a V-shaped area with the base of the "V" at the leaf midrib. Veins in these areas become dark brown or black; when the leaf is held up to a strong light source, they show up as a black net. Vascular tissue of the main stem then becomes blackened.

diagnostic_features.value: V-shaped yellow area at leaf margins with the base at the leaf midrib; dark brown or black veins forming a visible black net pattern when held to light; blackened vascular tissue in the main stem; bacterial streaming visible as a white substance exiting cut plant tissue when placed in water.
diagnostic_features.quote: Tissues at leaf margins become yellow; chlorosis progresses toward the leaf center, creating a V-shaped area with the base of the "V" at the leaf midrib. Veins in these areas become dark brown or black; when the leaf is held up to a strong light source, they show up as a black net. Vascular tissue of the main stem then becomes blackened.

look_alikes.quote: Fusarium wilt and Verticillium wilt can infect brassica crops, as well, and may be confused for black rot

conflicts.note: NC State source appears to contain a typographical error ('campetris' instead of 'campestris'); canonical spelling confirmed by PNW Handbooks and UMass sources.

conflicts.canonical_value: Leaves, Stem, Root, Vascular tissue, Whole plant, Seed
conflicts.alternative_value: Leaves, Stem, Root (no mention of seed or whole plant)
conflicts.note: UMass source does not explicitly list seed or whole plant among affected parts, though PNW Handbooks and NC State do.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Downy mildew on brassica crops is caused by the oomycete (fungal-like organism) Hyaloperonospora parasitica.

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the oomycete (fungal-like organism) Hyaloperonospora parasitica

affected_parts.quote: Small, angular lesions develop on leaves and inflorescences... gray streaks may form beneath the beads, running all the way back to the main stem... Turnip or radish roots may develop internal, irregularly shaped brown or black discoloration... systemic...pathogen is able to move from the lower leaves into the stem and head

summary.value: Small angular light green to yellow lesions develop on leaf surfaces and enlarge into irregularly-shaped necrotic patches, with gray to white spore masses appearing on the leaf undersurface. Under high humidity, grayish-white mycelial growth appears on the underside of leaf spots. Systemically infected plants develop black streaking and discoloration inside stems and heads.
summary.quote: Symptoms on older leaves appear as small, angular, light green to yellow lesions on the upper leaf surface. The lesions enlarge with the development of disease and form irregularly-shaped necrotic patches. On the undersurface of the leaf, gray to white masses of spores will develop ("downy" growth).

diagnostic_features.value: Distinctive gray to white downy masses of spores on the undersurface of leaves; under favorable conditions both sides of leaves may be covered with spores. Sunken black spots on cabbage heads may be minute or larger than 1 inch in diameter. Yellow lesions on leaves may have networks of black spots or lines throughout, appearing web-like.
diagnostic_features.quote: On the undersurface of the leaf, gray to white masses of spores will develop ("downy" growth). Under favorable conditions, both sides of the leaves may be covered with spores (sporangia and sporangiaphores).

value: Cold-damaged tissues with secondary leaf rot
look_alikes.quote: Other foliar diseases such as Alternaria blight, anthracnose, or bacterial leaf spot may be mistaken for downy mildew on brassica crops.

conflicts.note: UMass Extension uses 'Hyaloperonospora brassicae s.l.' while NC State and PNW Handbooks use 'Hyaloperonospora parasitica' (with PNW also noting the synonym Peronospora parasitica). No taxonomy validation was provided to resolve this conflict; canonical value follows NC State (higher authority extension source).
PNW Handbooks lists the name as Peronospora parasitica with Hyaloperonospora parasitica given as a synonym in parentheses.
PNW Handbooks describes the pathogen as 'a fungus-like microorganism', which could imply Fungal. NC State explicitly classifies it as an oomycete, which is the scientifically accurate classification.
